passages.text: A microcontroller combines a processor, memory and input/output pins on one chip. Arduino boards use AVR or ARM microcontrollers; the ESP32 adds built-in WiFi and Bluetooth. Firmware is usually written in C or C++.
The ESP32 is a low-cost microcontroller with WiFi and Bluetooth, popular for IoT projects. It has ADC inputs, PWM outputs, I2C, SPI and UART, and can sleep to save battery power.
A Raspberry Pi is a single-board computer that runs Linux. Compared with a microcontroller it has more memory and processing power, but it uses more power and is not real-time.
An interrupt makes the processor pause its main code to handle an event, such as a pin change or a timer, in a short interrupt service routine. Interrupts avoid constant polling.
Mechanical buttons bounce, producing several quick transitions per press. Debouncing filters these, in software with a short delay or timer, or in hardware with an RC filter and Schmitt trigger.
An analog-to-digital converter (ADC) samples a voltage and turns it into a number. Resolution, for example 10 or 12 bits, sets the smallest step it can measure; the reference voltage sets the range.
Pulse-width modulation (PWM) switches a pin on and off quickly; the duty cycle sets the average power. It is used to dim LEDs, control motor speed and position servo motors.
I2C is a two-wire bus (SDA data and SCL clock) that connects many devices by address. It needs pull-up resistors and is common for sensors and small displays.
SPI is a fast synchronous bus with separate clock, data-in, data-out and chip-select lines. It suits displays, SD cards and fast sensors.
UART is serial communication over TX and RX lines at an agreed baud rate. Serial prints over UART are a common way to debug firmware.
MQTT is a lightweight publish-subscribe protocol for IoT. Devices publish messages to topics on a broker, and other devices or servers subscribe to those topics.
An IoT system connects sensors and devices to a network so data can be monitored or controlled remotely, often through a cloud server, a database and a web or mobile dashboard.

Systematic debugging means reproducing the problem, isolating it by testing one part at a time, forming and testing a hypothesis, fixing it, then retesting the whole system. Tools include serial prints, debuggers, multimeters, oscilloscopes and logic analyzers.
Git is a version control system. It records changes as commits, lets team members work on branches, and merges their work; GitHub hosts Git repositories online.
Data structures such as arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, hash tables and trees organize data so programs can store and search it efficiently.
A database stores data so it can be queried. Relational databases such as MySQL or SQLite use tables and SQL; they are common in web systems and data logging projects.
A web system has a front end that runs in the browser (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) and a back end on a server that handles logic and the database.
An operating system manages processes, memory, files and devices. Concepts include scheduling, threads, and synchronization to avoid race conditions.
Machine learning trains a model on example data so it can make predictions. Projects usually involve collecting and labeling data, training, and testing accuracy on data the model has not seen.
An embedded system is a computer built into a device for a dedicated task, with limits on memory, power and timing. Some use a real-time operating system (RTOS) to schedule tasks.
Digital logic uses gates such as AND, OR, NOT, NAND and XOR. Combinational circuits depend only on current inputs; sequential circuits use flip-flops to store state.
An FPGA is a chip of configurable logic blocks programmed with a hardware description language such as Verilog or VHDL. It runs many operations in parallel.
Computers represent data in binary. Hexadecimal is a compact way to write binary values; two's complement represents negative integers.

Ohm's law relates voltage, current and resistance: voltage equals current times resistance. Kirchhoff's current law says currents into a node sum to zero; the voltage law says voltages around a loop sum to zero.
A voltage divider uses two resistors to produce a fraction of the input voltage. It is often used to scale a sensor or battery voltage down to an ADC's input range.
Decoupling capacitors placed close to a chip's power pins supply short current bursts and filter noise on the supply rail.
A transistor can act as a switch or an amplifier. A BJT is controlled by base current; a MOSFET by gate voltage. Microcontrollers use them to switch loads such as motors and relays.
An operational amplifier (op-amp) amplifies the difference between its inputs. With feedback resistors it forms inverting and non-inverting amplifiers, buffers and active filters.
A power supply converts and regulates voltage. Linear regulators are simple and quiet but waste power as heat; switching regulators (buck, boost) are more efficient but can add switching noise.
A relay is an electrically controlled switch for higher-power loads. Its coil is usually driven through a transistor with a flyback diode to protect the circuit.
A motor driver or H-bridge lets a low-power controller drive a motor in both directions. Servo motors take a PWM position signal; stepper motors move in fixed steps.

Noise in a sensor signal can be reduced in hardware with shielded or short wires, proper grounding, decoupling capacitors and RC or active low-pass filters, and in software with averaging, moving average or median filters.
A low-pass filter passes low frequencies and reduces high frequencies. A simple RC low-pass filter has a cutoff frequency of one over two pi R C.
The Nyquist theorem says a signal must be sampled at more than twice its highest frequency to avoid aliasing. An anti-aliasing low-pass filter is placed before the ADC.
A moving average filter replaces each reading with the average of the last few readings. It smooths random noise but adds a small delay.
Modulation puts information on a carrier wave. AM varies amplitude, FM varies frequency; digital schemes include ASK, FSK, PSK and QAM.
An antenna converts electrical signals to radio waves and back. Its size relates to the wavelength; gain, impedance matching and placement affect range.
Common short-range wireless links include WiFi, Bluetooth, Zigbee and LoRa. They trade off range, data rate and power use.
Fiber optic cables carry data as light, with low loss and immunity to electromagnetic interference; they are used in telecommunications networks.

PCB design involves a schematic, component footprints, placement and routing. Good practice includes a solid ground plane, short high-current and high-speed traces, enough trace width for the current, and decoupling capacitors near chips.
KiCad and Altium are PCB design tools; Proteus and Multisim simulate circuits before building them. Design rule checks catch spacing and connection errors before fabrication.
Good soldering joints are shiny and cone-shaped. Common faults are cold joints and solder bridges; a multimeter continuity test helps find them.

An oscilloscope shows how a voltage changes over time, revealing noise, timing and signal shape. A multimeter measures voltage, current, resistance and continuity; a logic analyzer captures digital signals and decodes buses.

Common sensors in student projects include ultrasonic distance sensors, temperature and humidity sensors, soil moisture sensors, flow sensors, PIR motion sensors and load cells. Calibration compares their readings with a reference.
Solar-powered projects use a solar panel, a charge controller and a battery. Power budgeting estimates how long the battery lasts from the average current draw.
Testing a project means checking each part separately (unit testing), then the whole system (integration testing), comparing results with expected values or a reference instrument.
Engineering documentation includes requirements, schematics, code comments, test results and user manuals, so others can use and maintain the work.
Electrical safety includes disconnecting power before changing wiring, using fuses, and separating low-voltage control circuits from mains voltage.
